Title: India's overseas investment commitments fall 37% to USD 4.34 billion in September: RBI
Description: India's overseas direct investment commitments declined by nearly 37 per cent to USD 4.34 billion in September 2026, compared with USD 6.87 billion in August, mainly due to a sharp fall in guarantees issued by Indian companies, according to data released by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Monday. According to the RBI's Summary of Outward Foreign Direct Investment (OFDI) based on Reporting Date - September 2026, guarantees issued by Indian companies for overseas investments fell sharply to USD 528.21 million in September from USD 2.29 billion in August, a decline of nearly 77 per cent. Equity commitments also declined to USD 3.27 billion in September from USD 4.11 billion in the previous month, representing a fall of around 20 per cent. However, equity commitments were nearly 26 per cent higher than the USD 2.59 billion recorded in September last year, indicating stronger year-on-year equity investment commitments despite the monthly slowdown. Meanwhile, loan commitments increased to USD 549.16 million in September from USD 473.52 million in August, registering a rise of nearly 16 per cent. The decline in overall overseas investment commitments was therefore largely driven by lower guarantees, rather than a uniform fall across all investment categories. The RBI stated that the data is provisional and subject to change based on online reporting by AD banks. Overseas financial commitments include equity investments, loans and guarantees provided by Indian entities to their foreign subsidiaries and joint ventures. These commitments do not necessarily represent actual cash outflows during the month. The latest figures come at a time when India's net foreign direct investment inflows have strengthened, supported partly by a moderation in outward investment. According to the RBI's October 2026 Bulletin, net FDI inflows increased to USD 13.8 billion during April-August FY27 from USD 9.6 billion in the corresponding period last year. Title: El Nino risks may push global food prices higher in 2027; full impact to emerge gradually: Report
Description: Global food prices could rise further in 2027 amid increasing fertilizer and farming costs, coupled with potential El Nino-related weather disruptions, with the impact likely to become more evident over the coming months, however, the full impact on food will take time to appear, according to a report by S&P Global. The report warned that an exceptionally strong El Nino could threaten agricultural production across major crop-producing regions, while shortages of fertilizer and diesel continue to put pressure on farmers. "The impact on food will likely become much more apparent over the next few months as farmers wrestle with high costs and with shortages of fertilizer and diesel." "Unlike changes in oil prices , which register immediately, the full impact on food will take time to appear. Farmers buy seed, fertilizer and fuel months before they sell a crop," it said, stressing, "The squeeze now bearing down on farm budgets may therefore not reach food markets in force until 2027." According to S&P Global, fertilizer production is expected to recover gradually, allowing markets to stabilise. Higher crop prices could improve farmers' profit margins, encourage more land to be brought under cultivation and increase fertilizer use. However, the adjustment will take time, with consumers likely to face higher food prices before agricultural production and supply recover. "Commodities other than the basic staples will be affected by the El Nino, including cash crops that are important to livelihoods in many poorer regions," it noted. To describe it further, the report noted, global agriculture is facing pressure from rising fertilizer and energy costs, growing demand for biofuels and potential El Nino-related weather disruptions. It highlighted that fertilizer production depends heavily on natural gas, while diesel is essential for operating farm machinery, irrigation systems and transporting agricultural produce. Rising energy prices are therefore increasing production costs and putting pressure on farmers' profit margins. "As the conflicts in Europe and the Middle East have driven up diesel prices, biofuels become more attractive. The knock-on effect is that, in some regions, crops for fuel become more valuable than crops for food." What is unfolding is not a single agricultural shock, but the convergence of several shocks. Conflict is moving through fertilizer, energy and biofuel markets, raising costs and narrowing farmers' choices just as an extreme El Nino threatens harvests. "An exceptionally strong El Nino, expected to peak in late 2026, acts as an environmental multiplier that threatens to unleash severe droughts and floods across key Asian, African and Latin American breadbaskets in 2027," it said. The impact could be particularly severe in regions where crop productivity has already been weakened by insufficient fertilizer use over successive growing seasons. S&P Global also warned that global grain reserves remain at historically low levels amid the ongoing Ukraine war, leaving limited capacity to absorb simultaneous crop failures across multiple regions. Overall, "A global food crisis is not foreordained. But neither is it any longer a distant risk," it added. (ANI)

She said the Centre was continuously taking measures to ensure that these developments did not adversely affect the public. Title: "Higher-than-usual turnout in left strongholds": Netanyahu urges his supporters as Israel records high early poll turnout
Description: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday (local time) urged right-wing voters to cast their ballots, claiming that turnout was higher than usual in left-wing strongholds. His remarks come as Israel recorded 16.7 per cent voter turnout by 10 am local time, the highest early polling figure at that hour since at least 1981, according to The Times of Israel. In a post on X, Netanyahu called on his supporters to vote, describing the situation as an "emergency hour" for right-wing voters. "Higher-than-usual turnout rates in the left's strongholds. Right or Palestine, for real. Right-wing voters, this is an emergency hour... Go out and vote right now!" he said. "The left's activists are storming the polling stations-and the right's activists are indifferent. This is the time to wake up. Go out and get others out to vote-vote Likud," he said in a follow-up post. According to the Central Elections Committee, voter turnout stood at 16.7 per cent as of 10 am local time, compared to 15.9 per cent at the same time during the 2022 election. The Times of Israel reported that around 1.2 million votes had been cast by that hour, is the highest turnout at this hour since 1981 - when Menachem Begin was reelected as prime minister. Meanwhile, Netanyahu's principal challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, visited Kibbutz Nir Oz, one of the communities hardest hit by the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack. Eisenkot walked alongside former hostage Gadi Mozes towards his polling booth before leaving to cast his own vote elsewhere. "I am proud and moved to begin this day with Gadi Mozes, a symbol of the Israeli spirit and strength, of Israelis' commitment to one another and their commitment to the state," Eisenkot told reporters, pledging to work towards healing and rebuilding the country. Mozes endured 482 days in Hamas captivity and campaigned for Eisenkot, a former Israel Defence Forces chief of staff who lost his son Gal and two nephews while they were fighting in Gaza during the war, The Times of Israel reported. President Isaac Herzog, meanwhile, visited the Central Election Committee headquarters and described the election as a celebration of democracy, urging citizens to exercise their right to vote. Following the counting of votes, Herzog will consult the leaders of elected parties before assigning a lawmaker the task of forming the next government. The designated candidate will have 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension. If the attempts fail, further options will be explored, and Israel could face another election if no government can be formed. (ANI)

Title: Miliband 'deeply concerned' after MPs say they were detained on way to West Bank
Description: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said he was “deeply concerned” after MPs said they were detained for eight hours by Israeli authorities and denied entry to the West Bank . Labour’s Clive Lewis and the SNP’s Lara Bird, along with MSP Kate Nevens of the Scottish Greens, said they were interrogated and denied access to the territory on Monday. Mr Miliband told the Commons on Tuesday that the Government has now raised the issue with the Israeli authorities. The MPs had travelled as part of a delegation organised by political group Progressive International. According to Progressive International, the group – which also included former MP Sam Tarry and Spanish senator Josu Estarrona Elizondo – was stopped while making the crossing from Jordan and had planned to undertake “a programme of meetings with Palestinian academics, students and civil society organisations” as well as join the olive harvest following what it claims are “mounting attacks” against farmers in the territory. In the Commons, Labour MP Dr Simon Opher (Stroud) asked if the Foreign Secretary would join him in condemning the MPs being blocked from entering the territory. Mr Miliband responded: “We are obviously deeply concerned about the denial of entry to the West Bank for two Members of Parliament, and I believe one member of the Scottish Parliament as well. “We have raised this issue with the Israeli authorities and been in touch with the MPs to offer assistance. “More broadly, it’s very, very important that members of this House, as they go about their business – not just in the UK but internationally – have free access so that they can actually do their duties.” In a post on X, Norwich South MP Mr Lewis said: “For more than eight hours, we were held, interrogated and made to feel as though we had done something wrong simply by attempting to enter. “The simple truth is we had done nothing wrong. “We went to show our support for the Palestinian people and highlight the terrible injustice and violence being perpetrated against them. “We want to ensure that people back home do not look away from the reality of what is happening. “Ultimately, we went to show solidarity. But we left with an even greater determination to speak out. “We will not be silenced, and we will not look away. None of us should.” Ms Bird – who was elected earlier this year to the Arbroath and Broughty Ferry seat on Scotland’s east coast – posted: “I came to stand alongside Palestinians being attacked for harvesting olives on their own land. Instead, we were turned away, with no reason given. “More than ever, Palestinians are being subject to terror and violence by the IDF and illegal settlers. “Increased blockades, demolitions and unthinkable violence have become the norm for Palestinians in the West Bank. “It is more important now than ever that we bear witness and show our solidarity.” Reports suggest the two MPs could have sought permission to access the West Bank from the Israeli government. Green MSP Ms Nevens added: “We had travelled to the West Bank to stand in solidarity with Palestinians facing escalating violence, and to join the olive harvesters. “We went to bear witness, to listen to Palestinian communities and to help shine a light on the abuses taking place. “The Israeli forces didn’t want us to see the demolished homes, or the settlers inflicting so much misery or the day to day indignities that are so central to the occupation.” The Foreign Office and Israeli embassy have been contacted for comment. Title: World Uyghur Congress warns of imminent 2 Uyghur men deportations from Thailand to China
Description: The World Uyghur Congress (WUC) has raised alarm over the imminent deportation of two Uyghur men from Thailand to China after they were granted royal pardons and transferred from regular detention to an immigration detention facility on October 21, warning that their return could expose them to torture and enforced disappearance. According to a press release issued by the WUC, the two men are among five Uyghurs who remain in detention in Thailand from a larger group of approximately 300 Uyghurs who fled persecution in China and were detained near the Thai-Malaysian border in March 2014. The organisation said that in 2015, Thai authorities deported 100 Uyghurs from the group to China. Those who remained were held for years in immigration detention centres under what the WUC described as de facto incommunicado detention. They were allegedly denied access to legal representation and non-governmental organisations, received inadequate medical care and nutrition, and had limited opportunities for physical exercise. Five members of the group died while in detention. The WUC further stated that in 2025, another 40 Uyghurs were deported to China despite widespread political and public opposition. According to the organisation, their families have been unable to establish contact with any of those deported, and neither Chinese nor Thai authorities have provided proof of life, even one year after their deportation. The organisation described the situation as enforced disappearance, alleging that the deported Uyghurs had effectively disappeared after being returned to China. Warning against the deportation of the remaining detainees, the WUC said Thailand would violate its international legal obligations if it returned the two men to a country where they could face serious risks of torture and enforced disappearance. The press release also highlighted the broader human rights situation in China, stating that since 2016, Uyghurs have faced mass incarceration, forced labour, torture in detention, forced sterilisation and family separation, affecting millions of people. Thailand must not deport these Uyghur refugees to China, as doing so risks making it complicit in the ongoing genocide against the Uyghurs, WUC President Turgunjan Alawdun said. He added that all countries had a responsibility to uphold international law and firmly reject the repression of Uyghurs, both within China and beyond its borders. The WUC also referred to Thailand's obligations under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), the Convention against Torture (CAT) and the International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance (ICPPED). According to the organisation, these international treaties impose obligations relevant to the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits returning individuals to countries where they face a risk of torture, other prohibited ill-treatment or enforced disappearance. The WUC called on Thailand to refrain from deporting the two Uyghur men and the remaining group of five detainees to China. It also urged third-country governments to offer resettlement opportunities to all five Uyghurs currently held in regular and immigration detention. Additionally, the organisation appealed to the European Union, the United Nations and governments of third countries to mobilise international pressure on Thailand to ensure that no Uyghur detainee is deported to China. (ANI)

Title: US delegation expected in Doha for direct Iran talks after reported breakthrough: Reports
Description: An American delegation is expected to join Iranian officials for direct talks in Doha following a reported breakthrough in indirect negotiations between Washington and Tehran, The Times of Israel reported, citing the Qatari newspaper Al-Araby Al-Jadeed. According to the report, citing sources close to mediation efforts led by Qatar and Pakistan, the two sides have reached an understanding on preliminary measures concerning Iran's nuclear programme, navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and financial incentives for Tehran. China and Russia are also reportedly expected to serve as guarantors of any agreement. The reported progress follows more than 12 hours of discussionsbetweenQatari mediators and Iranian officials in Tehran on Friday, aimed at restarting direct negotiations between Washington and Tehran and preventing a renewed outbreak of war, according to Axios. Citing diplomatic sources, Axios reported that the discussions were held amid growing concerns over a possible US military operation against Iran following the November 3 midterm elections. The talks are set to continue in Doha on Saturday. A diplomatic source told Axios that Qatari mediators remained in regular contact with the White House during Friday's discussions. "There was positive progress. Talks are still ongoing in an effort to unlock a deal between the US and Iran," the source said. Qatar is pushing both sides to agree on a series of reciprocal steps that could be implemented over a few days, paving the way for the resumption of direct negotiations on Iran's nuclear programme and other issues. However, differences over the conditions for restarting negotiations have continued to complicate the diplomatic efforts. According to a US official cited by Axios, the Trump administration wants Iran to make nuclear concessions as a condition for resuming talks, while Tehran has demanded that Washington first lift its naval blockade, release frozen funds and allow it to sell oil. Qatari mediators are also seeking to persuade Iran to allow United Nations inspectors to visit its bombed nuclear sites as a confidence-building measure, in return for possible sanctions relief from Washington. Meanwhile, a preliminary draft framework for US-Iran negotiations proposes transferring Iran's highly enriched uranium stockpile to an agreed third country or reducing its enrichment level, while reopening the Strait of Hormuz to international maritime traffic within seven days of an initial understanding, Al Arabiya English reported. According to Al Arabiya English, which exclusively obtained the draft's key points, China could potentially act as a guarantor for the implementation and sustainability of any agreement. The framework also proposes holding direct US-Iran negotiations in Doha instead of Istanbul. Under the proposed arrangement, Iran's measures on its nuclear programme and maritime security would be matched by US steps to ease sanctions, blockades and economic restrictions. An independent verification mechanism would assess compliance before each phase of implementation, ensuring that neither side makes substantial concessions without corresponding, independently verifiable commitments. The draft also proposes a dispute-resolution mechanism involving mediators and guarantor parties to address delays or violations and prevent renewed military escalation, according to the news platform. Meanwhile, divisions reportedly persist within US President Donald Trump's administration over the next course of action. US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are highly sceptical about the possibility of reaching a nuclear agreement with the current Iranian regime and favour further weakening it, including through additional strikes, a US official told Axios. In contrast, Vice President JD Vance and Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are in favour of resuming negotiations. Trump, however, remains sceptical about whether Tehran would accept an agreement meeting his expectations. "There are talks. They want to talk. They keep talking. ...We have time, frankly. It's a war, but it is not a typical war," Trump told reporters on Friday. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who is leading the administration's economic pressure campaign, dubbed "Operation Economic Outcast", is also among the senior officials urging Trump to allow the initiative to continue rather than rush into renewed military action, Axios reported. Regional countries, including Egypt, Turkey, Iraq, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, have also been pressing Iran to resume negotiations before the US midterm elections, according to a regional source cited by Axios. The diplomatic push comes amid concerns that a renewed conflict could trigger widespread destruction across Iran and the Gulf region, further worsening the global energy crisis. Iran has threatened to retaliate against any US strikes on its energy infrastructure by targeting oil and gas facilities in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait and Bahrain. According to Axios, any renewed US military operation against Iran would be conducted jointly with Israel, with Tehran likely to respond through missile strikes. Hezbollah could also launch attacks against Israel. Meanwhile, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is reportedly lobbying Trump to launch a joint military operation against Iran immediately after the US midterm elections, adding to the uncertainty surrounding the diplomatic efforts. (ANI)
